enrichment.short_title: Police officer's malicious prosecution claim struck out after rape charge discontinued
key_facts: PC McHarg, a Thames Valley police officer, was arrested on 19 July 1998 and charged with rape after a complainant reported non-consensual sex in his garage; CPS discontinued proceedings on 18 December 1998 because she would not give evidence.
In 2003 McHarg sued the Chief Constable for malicious prosecution, accepting the prosecution ended in his favour but alleging DI Colchester lacked reasonable and probable cause and acted maliciously.

The defendant applied for summary judgment under CPR 24.2, arguing the investigating officer's file to the CPS was fair, Dr Barker's sceptical views were included, and there was no affirmative evidence of dishonest belief or malice.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for summary judgment (and alternatively strike out) in the Queen's Bench Division before trial on a malicious prosecution claim.
enrichment.outcome: Summary judgment entered for the defendant; claim held to have no real prospect of success on reasonable and probable cause or malice.
enrichment.ratio: Want of reasonable and probable cause is for the judge and requires affirmative evidence of lack of honest belief before a jury question arises; where the CPS file fully disclosed Dr Barker's scepticism and the complainant's account supported prosecution, and there was no evidence the investigating officer concealed his own disbelief, a malicious prosecution claim cannot succeed at summary judgment.
legal_issues: Whether the police were the prosecutor for malicious prosecution purposes
Whether there was want of reasonable and probable cause for charging McHarg with rape
Whether DI Colchester acted without honest belief or with malice
Whether omissions from the report to the CPS (neighbour statements, Dr Barker visit) affected reasonable cause

enrichment.short_title: Parole Board damages withheld from lifer unlawfully at large pending surrender
key_facts: Mr Ram, convicted of murder with an 11-year tariff, settled judicial review proceedings against the Parole Board for £20,000 by Tomlin order in April 2003 for unlawful detention between November 2000 and June 2002.
After costs set-offs, £1,000 remained outstanding; in May 2003 his licence was revoked after he disappeared and he remained unlawfully at large.

The Secretary of State offered payment only by personal collection at a police station; Ram sought payment to his solicitors, and the Secretary of State applied to set aside or vary the consent order.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to set aside or vary a Tomlin consent order and related enforcement/specific performance application in judicial review proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Application to set aside or vary the consent order refused; court exercised discretion under Crown Proceedings Act 1947 s 25(3) to suspend payment of any balance to the claimant personally while unlawfully at large, protecting solicitors' and Legal Services Commission interests.
enrichment.ratio: A claimant's recall and failure to surrender after release on licence is foreseeable and not a Barder supervening event justifying variation of a consent damages order; nevertheless the court may suspend Crown payment under s 25(3) where paying damages would assist a person unlawfully at large, without denying the underlying liability.
legal_issues: Whether damages under a Tomlin order must be paid while the claimant is unlawfully at large
Whether an implied term or Barder variation could withhold payment
How CLS Regulations and the Access to Justice Act first charge interact with enforcement
Whether specific performance or s 25 certificate procedure was appropriate

enrichment.short_title: Parents' appeal dismissed over autistic child's ABA programme versus Pines School placement
key_facts: H, a five-year-old girl with autism, was the subject of a statement of special educational needs maintained by Birmingham City Council.

Parents sought continuation of a home-based Lovaas/ABA programme; the SEND Tribunal ordered placement at the Pines School with 32.5 hours intensive support, rejecting an extended school day as unsupported by research and disproportionately costly.
On statutory appeal Sir Richard Tucker held the tribunal's reasoning lawful, adequately reasoned, and sufficiently specific.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Statutory appeal under section 11 of the Tribunals and Inquiries Act 1992 against a Special Educational Needs and Disability Tribunal decision; permission to appeal refused orally at the end of the hearing.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; permission to appeal refused on section 9/319 and specificity grounds.
enrichment.ratio: A specialist SEND Tribunal's decision that a named special school can meet a child's needs is entitled to deference; where appropriate school-based provision exists, section 319 does not require home-based education, and Part 3 of a statement may lawfully allow flexible transitional arrangements without unlawful delegation.
legal_issues: Whether the tribunal misapplied research evidence on extended ABA provision
Whether section 9 parental wishes and section 319 'education otherwise' required a home-based ABA programme
Whether the tribunal's order lacked sufficient specificity in Part 3
Whether fresh evidence of tribunal proceedings was admissible on appeal

enrichment.short_title: Kitchen buyer lost right to reject mismatched pine units after delay and use

statutes_considered.title: Supply of Goods and Services Act 1982

key_facts: The Joneses contracted with Gallery Kitchens in February 2000 for a handmade pine kitchen to match existing furniture for £8,645; installation completed by early May 2000.

They complained on 9 May 2000 about colour mismatch and other defects, allowed remedial work through September 2000, then removed the kitchen in about October 2000 and issued proceedings in October 2001 seeking full price recovery.
The district judge found breach of description and implied terms but held the buyers had accepted the goods and lost the right to reject; damages of £2,500 were awarded.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal with leave from Wrexham County Court against findings on acceptance under section 35 Sale of Goods Act 1979.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed with costs; finding that a reasonable time had elapsed before rejection was upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 35(4)–(6) Sale of Goods Act 1979, whether a reasonable time has passed before rejection is a question of fact; time spent requesting repairs does not automatically preserve rejection rights, and delay after patent colour defects and continued use can amount to deemed acceptance.
legal_issues: Whether the buyers lost the right to reject under section 35(1)(b) by acts inconsistent with the seller's ownership
Whether a reasonable time had elapsed under section 35(4) before rejection was intimated
How section 35(6) treats periods of repair and complaint
Whether Clegg v Andersson precluded loss of rejection rights during remedial correspondence

key_facts: Ms Aryan, an 18-year-old Iranian national who did not speak English, was charged with theft from John Lewis and initially appeared without legal aid.

Whether the defendant understood the nature and significance of electing summary trial

enrichment.short_title: Evangelical preacher convicted under section 5 for anti-homosexuality placard in Bournemouth
key_facts: Harry Hammond, an evangelical Christian preacher, displayed a double-sided sign in Bournemouth town centre on 13 October 2001 bearing 'Stop Immorality', 'Stop Homosexuality' and 'Stop Lesbianism'.

A crowd of 30–40 people gathered; soil was thrown, the placard was used to hit someone, and water was poured on Hammond; police asked him to leave and arrested him for breach of the peace when he refused.
He was prosecuted under section 5 Public Order Act 1986; magistrates found the sign insulting, that he was aware it might be, and that his conduct was not reasonable; fined £300.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of amended case stated to the Divisional Court after Hammond's death, pursued by his executors against conviction under section 5.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction upheld; appellant ordered to pay respondent's costs.
enrichment.ratio: Section 5 Public Order Act 1986 must be applied compatibly with Article 10 ECHR; words implying homosexuality and lesbianism are immoral may be found insulting as a fact, and where a preacher knowingly displays such a sign in a busy town centre provoking disorder, the section 5(3)(c) reasonableness defence fails as a proportionate restriction on expression.
legal_issues: Whether the sign was threatening, abusive or insulting within section 5(1)(b)
Whether Hammond was aware the sign might be insulting under section 6(4)
Whether prosecution was a justified and proportionate interference with Articles 9 and 10 ECHR
Whether Article 9 religious proselytism altered the Article 10 balance
Whether authorities should protect the speaker rather than arrest him when violence came from others

enrichment.short_title: Underpinning contractor denied summary judgment against housing association for insurer's unpaid share
key_facts: Family Housing Association owned 27 Muswell Hill; subsidence repairs were agreed between FHA, insurers Aegon (53%) and Independent (18%), and loss adjusters Cunningham Lindsay, with FHA liable for 29%.
Concrete Foundations Ltd completed underpinning in 2001 after engineers accepted its tender 'on behalf of our clients'; Aegon later refused indemnity and FHA paid only its 47% share.
The contractor sued FHA for the remaining 53%, arguing Cunningham Lindsay had ostensible authority to bind FHA for the full sum or that FHA was unjustly enriched.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Queen's Bench Division against Central London County Court's refusal of the claimant's application for summary judgment under CPR 24.2.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; matter not suitable for summary judgment; trial needed on agency, reliance and unjust enrichment.
enrichment.ratio: Actual authority of loss adjusters to commission work for an insured's apportioned share does not without more establish ostensible authority to bind the building owner for an insurer's share; whether a contractor relied on the principal and to whom credit was given are factual questions unsuitable for summary determination.
legal_issues: Whether Cunningham Lindsay had actual or ostensible authority to bind FHA for the full repair cost
Whether an agent could represent both insurer and insured where insurers withheld underwriting concerns
Whether FHA was unjustly enriched by the completed underpinning
To whom the contractor gave credit and whether it relied on representations by FHA

enrichment.short_title: Child blinded after tripping on hoggin path in council community garden — no liability
key_facts: Jade Kidd, aged 10, tripped on a loose stone on a hoggin path while running in Portsmouth City Council's fenced community garden attached to a care home on 11 May 2001, suffering total loss of sight in her left eye.
The garden had lawns and paths but no play equipment; ball games were prohibited; children regularly played there unsupervised.
The path section had been laid three months earlier, inspected as satisfactorily compacted; the council admitted she tripped on a stone.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from Portsmouth County Court dismissal of occupiers' liability claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed with costs; council not liable.
enrichment.ratio: A community garden used by children is not a designated children's playground; the occupier's duty under the 1957 Act is fact-sensitive, and hoggin paths matching existing surfaces were not shown to be unsuitable or improperly compacted merely because children played and ran there.
legal_issues: What standard of care applied to a community garden where children played unsupervised
Whether hoggin was an unsuitable surface where children were expected to run
Whether the path was inadequately compacted
Whether playground safety standards should be imported by analogy

enrichment.short_title: Wife refused permission to appeal revocation of £30,000 ancillary relief lump sum
key_facts: After a long marriage, Deputy District Judge Evans ordered Dr Waiwaiku to transfer the matrimonial home and insurance policies to his former wife, share pensions 50:50, pay £30,000 lump sum and £1,350 monthly periodical payments.
The husband appealed; HHJ Yelton set aside the £30,000 lump sum but upheld periodical payments, finding the husband could not raise further capital given existing debts of about £20,000.

The wife sought permission to appeal, alleging concealed capital and under-declared income, but the district judge had rejected her £116,000 'missing savings' allegation and credited both parties' Form E disclosures.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal against partial allowance of husband's appeal on ancillary relief lump sum order.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal and stay refused; no point of principle and no prospect of success identified.
enrichment.ratio: Lump sums in ancillary relief are ordinarily payable from available capital not borrowing capacity; where a judge has made clear credibility findings against a wife on non-disclosure and an appeal judge concludes the lump sum was unsupported on the evidence, permission to appeal requires a point of principle or cogent reason and will not be granted to retry disputed facts without new hard evidence.
legal_issues: Whether HHJ Yelton erred in setting aside the £30,000 lump sum order
Whether the husband failed to give full and frank financial disclosure
Whether lump sums may properly be ordered from borrowing capacity rather than capital
Whether increased NHS income justified revisiting the order
